title: "We engage with all kinds of art without requiring a clear single interpretation and meaning, but for some reason that's the way most people like to engage with film" - Thomas Flight (from his video on David Lynch)

commenti.body:
I feel like this same problem does exist in literature, at least in literary fiction, but not in visual art or music, because they generally deal with stories whereas the other artistic media do not. A piece of music can make you feel certain things, but it generally doesn't tell any kind of story, unless maybe it's an opera or something. A work of visual art, especially something made after the mid 20th century, doesn't necessarily have to tell a story or even contain any recognizable figures. That really opens them up to all kinds of interpretations, because there's nothing that seems concrete. It's all very nebulous, and deals more with feelings and emotions than it does any kind of facts or information. There are of course arguments about how much the artist's intent matters, but in the end everyone realizes you can feel feelings and have emotions without knowing any of that.

Film and literature, on the other hand, deal with stories, which generally are expected to contain facts about what happened, who did what, and maybe why they did it. The interpretation, then, seems to rest entirely on the facts of the story and not only what they mean, but why it is that someone is telling it to you. There doesn't seem to be as much room for interpretation, because how could anyone have more than one reason for telling you something? How could someone doing a particular thing in a story mean more than one thing? Because of what the focus is on, the story, people don't realize that you can just feel the emotions and feelings that come out of the film or book and just ignore the story entirely if you want, and just treat it like a piece of music. 

That's actually why David Lynch, and other surrealist filmmakers, are so great. The story can't matter because it doesn't make any sense. It's so disjointed that you kind of have to ignore it and just feel what it makes you feel.

Besides experimental films and shorts that are meant for museums, general audiences (and Lynch's work occasionally crosses into the mainstream) expect a somewhat traditional narrative from a movie - one that can be followed and understood in a way that music, painting, sculpture, and dance can not. 

If we look at the art forms that are more narrative-based, literature is more flexible and theater is open to certain allegories and suspension of belief that the realistic shape of movies usually don’t allow. So IMO people will either reject Lynch's work for being too inaccessible, or will try to make sense of what they watched based on an expectation that the filmmaker HAD to have a point, and one's interpretation must be it.

I think sometimes people hang into their own interpretations as a way to not conclude the movie was pointless and had nothing to say.

I don't believe that the people who are open to multiple interpretations in other art forms are necessarily the same people who seek to find a single correct interpretation of a film. Cinema is inherently a more populist medium than most other forms of art and therefore has a wider audience. This general audience more or less views cinema as mass entertainment and not as something to be engaged with critically.

Beyond the audience itself, the way we interact with cinema through social media, reviews from publications etc. do also have an effect of forming a general consensus on a movie. Also, directors and cast/crew end up doing incredible amounts of press for movies, giving precious insight. Whatever the artists say could be used to give credence to a particular interpretation. This kind of access isn't universal in other art forms.

Just because a creator not reveal/knowing the interpretation of a work /a part of a work , does not mean it doesnt have one most reasonable.

( Or you can claim there is infinite interpretation , but I would just say that is people weighting in too much of the involvement of themselves into an artwork in modern era )

David Lynch movies are all about his own mind. They're weird because HE'S weird. He called Straight Story his "most experimental" film because it's not about any part of his own soul or experiences. That's all he meant by that. And Eraserhead is his "most spiritual" because it's about his own life.

But I'm only saying that to reach the word limit. **Film mimics consciousness** more than any existing form of art. This triggers us. Seriously, we're triggered. Pissed off. You can rarely experience somebody else's consciousness and just be like "I have no problem with this". Other kinds of art used to piss people off, music still does, but now it's mostly film

Most people want life to have a point. It shouldn't be too surprising when they want their art to have a point, too. If something is open to infinite interpretation, then it's sort of the equivalent of saying "everything is true, nothing is false," which means truth is not meaningful anymore, and so any given interpretation is not meaningful anymore.

Which is to say, I think you can get most people to agree that there are not unlimited interpretations of any given work, or that at least, there are not unlimited interpretations that can be justified. Whether one interpretation can be justified, or several, is just a difference of degree, but we already agree that *some* interpretations must be wrong. It's inevitable that some people will continue to whittle down which interpretations are right, and probably end up with just the one in most cases.

And then, of course, people want to be right, people are *obsessed* with being right, and getting other people to agree with their worldview. This instinct naturally favors one interpretation, and can perhaps make all of us, at some point in our lives, hew so firmly to our own interpretation that we blind ourselves to others. 

So... yeah, it's complicated. Or maybe the explanation is much more simple: any given work is meaningful to the person who created it, and those of us who experience that work want to know what it meant to them. Maybe that's part of the magic of art: it's able to communicate something that might otherwise be ineffable, between creator and audience, and we want to be part of that conversation. We want to know that we are truly included.

Why? Because most film lovers are not very adept at actual, literal critical thinking.

I don't say that to be mean, it's just a fact as far as I'm concerned.

If you tried to explain the theory that authorial intent is just as valid an interpretation of art as any other theory that relies upon context from within the art itself, you'd be met with a lot of blank stares.

If you asked the average modern film lover to explain what makes art "sublime," they'd probably say "you mean that band from the 90s?"

They can't understand that there are always multiple valid interpretations of art coexisting simultaneously, and they can't understand it because they have never actually learned real, literal, legitimate critical theory.

What most people today consider a "fair critique" would make Pauline Kael blush.

I personally think most people are too obsessed with plots when they watch films, so they try to understand every film in a linear, methodical way and are desperate for the film makers to tell them exactly what happens and why.

In reality, the most important parts of films and what makes them interesting is the characters. The plot is just there to develop the characters, move things along and is often irrelevant, but people prefer to fixate on that as opposed to explore the human interactions, experiences and emotions, that lend for more open, interesting and nuanced discussions.

> We (or many of us) are open to multiple interpretations of music, painting, sculpture, dance and other art forms?

I’d argue this premise is simply wrong from the start. People are really not open to different interpretations to music, they don’t even understand the blatant intended meaning half the time, i.e. Springsteen’s, Born in the USA, the entire RATM catalog.  Most people don’t actually look for music to have multiple meanings, let alone even one meaning.

And the rejection of abstract art as having no meaning at all, or an obtuse one is probably the most well known and common reaction to modern art.

I’d wager most people don’t think dance means anything, rather than it meaning something and maybe even multiple somethings.

As far as film, people are trained to believe stories have a message, if the message is confusing, difficult or challenging, the initial reaction is likely to be that the story wasted their time, like a long winded speaker and their listener wanting them to “get to the point.”

This is the issue with any art.. people seem to want to find the "right" or "correct" interpretations.. why, I still don't know. It's nice to engage, exchange and connect over what we interpret personally.. but people seem quite severe about the "right" interpretation. And, this is what I turn away from..

Any indulgence in art - as the spectator, is actually quite deeply personal, for me atleast. It's always good to know the socio-cultural-political backgrounds, symbolisms, etc, I do enjoy analysing those, but after that, I think we should give way for more subjective and experiential aspect of our personal viewing of art.

This is the best thing about it... No two people see any art the same way if they stop trying to find the "right" interpretation, and allow themselves to be taken by it.. it could mean many things to just one person, in one viewing, in different viewings, in different moods, in different perspectives, different stages of life.. The world of art is the only place you can set your mind-heart-soul free, and look into it - indulge with it howsoever you can, want to, feel inclined to, feel drawn to.. and here we have so many people that are still putting it all in a box.. which is not even their own.. I wish people just set themselves free while engaging with art and come from their hearts about how they felt while seeing or listening to something, no matter how crazy or out there it may be...

His films are like Rorschach test. It is made create a vision but not so concrete one. His film are immersive because like a Rorschach, it is made to look like something familiar BUT not verging into familiarity. Have some sort of pattern or symmetric form  BUT in the end, it is just blots. It leaves spaces for you to fill in. 

Literature has a lot of this. Definitely art too. 

Finding meaning is always been a predilection of man. Sciences are built on understanding fundamentally anything under the sun into repeatable studies or observation. Its quite common for us, human to not like not knowing to be honest. Its a primal thing.

This kind of makes this kind of text (of Lynch, or the Post Impressionist to the Abstract) much more powerful because you can see it through multiple lens AND still be different. It  is ultimately all correct at best and can be all wrong at worst - which critics and cinephiles love to write in long passages. But the biggest and probably hardest thing is that in the end, a study or technical writing must have a gist, a thesis - ultimately limits the infinite interpretations into some logical sense that speaks to the writer and maybe others.

In short, we watch and ultimately need to make sense of things. Its impossible to say its not right or wrong interpretation from the author itself BUT It will definitely fall either into popularity/consensus or not, which will become the standard for acceptance.

> Springsteen’s, Born in the USA, the entire RATM catalog.

This. It is absolutely possible to have wrong interpretations of music.

Just because a person chooses to ignore the lyrical content of music does not mean that their interpretation of a song is correct.

It doesn't matter if you feel like Born in the USA is a pro-American pop song, it is actually an anti-war protest song about how the United States fails to take care of its veterans.

Killing in the Name Of is a critique against white supremacy in politics and police. Politicians and police constantly miss the point of the song, but that does not mean their interpretation is equally valid.
For people in the bubble of the online film world, looking at the online gaming community is a good parallel. They have an even harder time with this.

One of the things that I'm grateful for in Lynch is that he has popularised the whole idea of appreciating something in a way that doesn't require adherence to a linear storyline. 

Before him, practicioners of this form like Luis Buñuel, Wojciech Jerzy Has, and even later Tarkovsky, were definitely on the margins, appreciated by cinephiles but unheard-of by popular audiences.

Lynch's surreal touches in his early films and Twin Peaks helped popularize a style of film-appreciation, more than film-making, that has blossomed today. 

So it is that clearly dream-logic works like ***Everything Everywhere All At Once, Lanb, Border*** and ***Beau is Afraid*** can reach wider audiences than the surreal masters of the 1970s and earlier could have dreamed. It's not ***Fast and Furious*** size audiences, but still much greater than this style had before Lynch.

You're asking a bunch of film lovers who generally are open to multiple interpretations of stories and even completely "meaningless" stories.

If you want to know why ordinary folk like linear stories with closed definitive meanings, ask them. Surely you have a parent or grandparent, cousin or sibling who thinks "weird films/stories are shit". Ask them why they think so.

My own feeling is that they have closed off the childlike part of their imaginations which is open to dreamstates as a result of teaching - expectations of what being an adult is about, logical, coherent, goal driven.

If you pretend that people view films at random then this comment makes sense. But we don’t do that. Even most cinephiles that watch “arthouse” films still only watch entirely or an overwhelming majority of films in one style: narrative.

In your OP you mentioned that this happens to literature, as well - but oftentimes when we think of literature we think of “narrative literature”, which is also not all of writing.

As such, we are often self-selecting a certain form of art. I don’t think it’s that controversial to say that narrative art is, at is most basic, an elemental form of communication which has an intended meaning. Thus, it is pretty obvious why we would infer that there is some meaning, because that is the form. If we started from free association instead of narrative that would not be the case.

Then, add on 1,000,000 layers of cultural hegemony and lowest-common-denominator works of art and we almost entirely encounter narrative works of art that have clear and simple interpretations. There’s nothing inherently wrong with that - you can’t have satire without something to directly satirize, after all - but it does not represent the entirety of art’s possibilities. And that can be a bit boring. But it’s not surprising that it is the default.

Why people don’t stray from the default changes from person to person and even from moment to moment for any person - maybe they’re not well educated in the possibilities of the arts, maybe they’re not interested, maybe they’re tired at that given moment.

Basically, the answer to this guy’s question is blatantly obvious and I bet it’s also true even for him. Cultural hegemony is a real thing, after all. And our society is structured toward work and production for decreasing pay, not the enrichment of life through the arts, so it’s not going to get better.

Sure.

It's entirely possible for two critics to come to different conclusions about the meaning or quality of a film. 

If you can prove what you're saying about a movie is true using context from within the film itself, then your opinion/critique is **not wrong**, even if some people don't agree with you or have come to different conclusions about what the movie means or its quality using evidence from the film to back up their claims.

Ironically, some critics are good enough at what they do that they literally use this to their advantage and intentionally come up with ridiculous interpretations of a film just to annoy people.

Armond White was kind of a master at doing this, which is why he is now almost universally reviled, but like...if you read his criticisms? He almost always uses context and evidence from the film itself to make his case, which is how honest and legitimate criticism is done, so even though his takes were intended to defy expectations and piss people off, you couldn't necessarily say he was wrong. He was citing the source, proving his point almost every time. He's the kind of critic you hate because he's right for all the wrong reasons.

Enough films/movies lack ambiguity or the possibility of multiple interpretations for large swathes of the population to have become essentially "infantilised" into thinking that when the end credits of a film roll, no stones should be left unturned in terms of their apprehension of them. 

In short, the culture of movies itself is ultimately to blame.
